audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet final Jerusalem siege, Zedekiah capture and blinding, temple and city destruction, executions and exile, Gedaliah governorship and assassination, flight to Egypt, and Jehoiachin release narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for siege chronology, famine, military flight, Zedekiah's capture, killing of his sons before him, blinding and restraints, urban and temple burning, wall destruction, mass deportation, poor agricultural laborers left, cultural extraction, Riblah executions, colonial governorship, political assassination, refugee flight to Egypt, and Jehoiachin's limited elevation in Babylon.

verses.restored: In ninth year of his reign, in tenth month, on tenth of month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem. He camped against it and built siege works around it.
City entered siege until eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
On ninth of fourth month famine was strong in city, and there was no bread for people of land.
City was breached, and all men of war fled by night by way of gate between two walls by king's garden, while Chaldeans surrounded city. The king went by way toward Arabah.
Army of Chaldeans pursued king and overtook him in plains of Jericho; all his army scattered from him.
They seized king and brought him up to king of Babylon at Riblah, and they spoke judgments against him.
They slaughtered sons of Zedekiah before his eyes; then they blinded eyes of Zedekiah, bound him with bronze restraints, and brought him to Babylon.
In fifth month, on seventh of month, which was nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan chief of guards, servant of king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned house of YHWH, king's house, and all houses of Jerusalem; every great house he burned with fire.
All army of Chaldeans with chief of guards tore down walls around Jerusalem.
Remaining people left in city, deserters who had fallen to king of Babylon, and rest of multitude, Nebuzaradan chief of guards exiled.
But chief of guards left some of poorest of land as vineyard workers and field workers.
Bronze pillars in house of YHWH, stands, and bronze sea in house of YHWH Chaldeans broke apart and carried their bronze to Babylon.
Pots, shovels, snuffers, spoons, and all bronze vessels with which they ministered, they took.
Firepans and bowls—what was gold as gold and what was silver as silver—chief of guards took.
Two pillars, one sea, and stands Solomon made for house of YHWH—the bronze of all these vessels was beyond weighing.

Height of one pillar was eighteen cubits, and capital upon it was bronze; height of capital was three cubits, with lattice and pomegranates upon capital all around, all bronze. Like these was second pillar with lattice.
Chief of guards took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah second priest, and three guardians of threshold.

From city he took one officer appointed over men of war, five men seeing face of king who were found in city, scribe of commander of army who mustered people of land, and sixty men from people of land found in city.
Nebuzaradan chief of guards took them and brought them to king of Babylon at Riblah.
King of Babylon struck them and put them to death at Riblah in land of Hamath. Thus Judah was exiled from upon its land.
Over people remaining in land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon left, he appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan.

All commanders of armies, they and their men, heard that king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah. They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah son of Maacathite, they and their men.
Gedaliah swore to them and their men and said to them, Do not fear servants of Chaldeans. Live in land, serve king of Babylon, and it will be well for you.

In seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elishama, from royal seed, came, and ten men with him. They struck Gedaliah, and he died, along with Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.
All people, from small to great, and commanders of armies arose and came to Egypt, for they feared Chaldeans.

In thirty-seventh year of exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in twelfth month, on twenty-seventh of month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in year he became king, lifted head of Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison.
He spoke good things with him and set his throne above thrones of kings who were with him in Babylon.
He changed garments of his imprisonment, and Jehoiachin ate bread continually before him all days of his life.
His allowance was a continual allowance given to him from king, a day's portion in its day, all days of his life.

translation_notes: The siege lasts into a devastating famine. Starvation is a weapon and consequence of war, not proof that hungry civilians lacked faith or deserved suffering.
Zedekiah's sons are killed before his eyes, then he is blinded and restrained. This is torture designed to combine bereavement, sensory injury, humiliation, and captivity.
Blindness and disability are not the shame in verse 7; deliberate mutilation and imperial cruelty are. Disabled people must never be used as symbols of moral blindness or ruined masculinity.
Burning temple, palace, and homes and destroying city walls are cultural, religious, domestic, and civic devastation—not merely fulfillment or architectural change.
Those left as vineyard and field workers are called poorest of land. They retain full dignity and become coerced survivors responsible for food production amid destroyed institutions.
Temple bronze and vessels are dismantled and transferred. Material detail preserves the scale of cultural extraction and the loss of collective craft heritage.
Priests, officials, military personnel, a scribe, and sixty people are transported to Riblah and executed. Captive killing without due process remains atrocity.
Gedaliah governs under Babylonian appointment. His advice may be pragmatic survival under occupation, not free political consent or endorsement of empire.
Ishmael's royal descent does not legitimate assassination. His killing of Gedaliah, Judeans, and Chaldeans destabilizes the surviving community.
The flight to Egypt is refugee movement caused by credible fear of imperial reprisal. Displaced people must not be condemned for seeking safety.
Jehoiachin's release, changed clothing, table access, and daily allowance improve one prisoner's conditions but do not end exile, empire, dependence, or the suffering of the wider community.
Kings, Jeremiah, Chronicles, Ezekiel, and Babylonian evidence contain chronological and numerical differences requiring source-witness audit.
safety_note: Do not romanticize siege, starvation, child killing, blinding, cultural destruction, captive execution, occupation, assassination, or exile. Do not stigmatize disability or poverty, and do not condemn refugees who flee to Egypt. The book ends with limited dignity restored to one prisoner—not with empire defeated or collective trauma resolved.
